title: From Statistical Relational to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence: a Survey
extended_summary:
This paper is a survey that compares two branches of AI concerned with combining learning and reasoning: statistical relational AI (StarAI) and neurosymbolic AI (NeSy). The central question is how these communities represent logical knowledge, how they perform inference, how they handle uncertainty, and how they train systems that mix symbolic and subsymbolic components. Rather than reporting an empirical study, the paper organizes prior work into a common conceptual framework.

The authors identify seven shared dimensions for characterizing systems across the two areas: proof-based versus model-based inference, logical syntax, semantics, learning scope, representational form, integration of logic/probability/neural paradigms, and task type. They use these dimensions to position representative systems such as ProbLog, Markov Logic Networks, PSL, DeepProbLog, LTN, SBR, NeuralLP, and others. The survey explains how directed/proof-based methods compile logic into neural architectures, while model-based approaches use logic as a constraint or loss function.

Because this is a theory/review paper, it does not study a student population, classroom setting, or educational intervention. Its contribution is conceptual: it clarifies similarities and differences between StarAI and NeSy and argues that cross-fertilization between the fields can improve modularity, generalization, interpretability, and scalability. The paper also highlights open research challenges, including the trade-off between control and interpretability versus scalability in neurosymbolic methods.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual survey paper on neurosymbolic and statistical relational AI, not an empirical evaluation in K-12 education. It does not report an intervention study, participant sample, or outcomes, so there is no evaluative methodology to assess for evidence quality.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides background taxonomy and theoretical synthesis only; it does not test a technology intervention, report student outcomes, or estimate impact on learning or safety. No K-12 effect size or outcome evidence is presented.
